name: Sagittarius
introduction: is the Archer, a centaur drawing a bow aimed at the heart of the Scorpion. Its brightest stars form a teapot shape, easily recognized, with the Milky Way rising like steam from its spout. As a zodiac constellation, it contains the point where the Sun lies at the December solstice.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Looking toward Sagittarius, you are looking toward the center of our galaxy, about 26,000 light-years away. Hidden behind dust lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole about four million times the mass of the Sun. Tracking the stars orbiting it earned a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of its shadow.
This direction is also where the Milky Way is densest. Its star clouds are so rich that Sagittarius contains more Messier objects than any other constellation: 15 nebulae and star clusters.

image.caption: Star View schematic · catalogue positions, north up and east left
image.alt: The Teapot of Sagittarius points from its spout toward the Galactic Centre and Sagittarius A*, about 26,000 light-years away.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Kaus Australis](hip:90185), at the bottom of the teapot, is the brightest star. Above it are [Kaus Media](hip:89931) and [Kaus Borealis](hip:90496), the lid, and [Alnasl](hip:88635), the tip of the spout. [Nunki](hip:92855) and [Ascella](hip:93506) form the handle.

The Greek letters do not follow brightness: [Rukbat](hip:95347), Alpha Sagittarii, is only of fourth magnitude, outshone by more than a dozen other stars of the Archer. [X Sagittarii](hip:87072), just beyond the spout, is a Cepheid variable, a pulsating supergiant that brightens and fades every seven days.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Sagittarius is a showcase of deep-sky objects: the Lagoon Nebula (M8) and Trifid Nebula (M20), glowing clouds of star birth visible in binoculars; the Omega Nebula (M17); the bright globular cluster M22; and the Sagittarius Star Cloud (M24). Behind the Milky Way’s core, the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy is being torn apart and absorbed by our galaxy.
